title: Who Thinks Best Depends on How Long You Let Them
hook: Change the token budget and the leaderboard changes with it. Model rankings reversed on every benchmark tested — which means a single-budget eval is measuring the budget as much as the model.
key_points: Varied the maximum generation budget across seven levels (64–4,096 tokens) for four models on three reasoning benchmarks — 56,476 inferences.
Model rankings reversed across budgets on all three benchmarks (McNemar, p < 0.01).
3–19% of items are non-monotone: accuracy drops as the budget grows, even after controlling for truncation.
Non-monotonicity is model-specific — only 6–14% of those items overlap between models.
Oracle model-selection analysis shows complementarity worth up to +27.8 points, largest at constrained budgets.
A budget-aware router recovered 14.1% of that oracle gap cross-domain; budget features helped in-domain but hurt transfer.
content_html: Benchmarks quietly assume that if model A beats model B, it beats it under any reasonable inference setting. Rodrigo Guedes de Souza and Alison R. Panisson (arXiv, August 2026) tested that by sweeping the token generation budget — the cap on how much a model may produce — across seven levels from 64 to 4,096 tokens, over four models and three reasoning benchmarks, for 56,476 total inferences.
extra_html:
The findings

Rankings reversed across budgets on all three benchmarks (McNemar, p < 0.01). Between 3% and 19% of items were non-monotone — accuracy actually fell as the model was permitted to think longer — and this persisted after controlling for truncation. Which items misbehave is model-specific, with only 6–14% overlap across models.

That model-specificity is also an opportunity. An oracle that picks the best model per item captures up to +27.8 percentage points, and the gap is widest at tight budgets. The authors' budget-aware router recovers 14.1% of that oracle gap across domains; budget features gave +1.6 to +5.7 points within a domain but cost -1.2 points when transferred, so they don't generalize for free.

Why it matters

If a leaderboard fixes one budget, it is partly measuring that budget. The authors argue for budget-conditioned evaluation protocols — and, for anyone deploying, for checking that your model choice still holds at the token limit you actually run in production.

related.title: Can We Trust Item Response Theory for AI Evaluation?
related.hook: IRT ranks models off a handful of items instead of averaging accuracy — but the math was built for human test-takers, and AI benchmarks break its assumptions in ways that quietly distort rankings.

related.title: Do Agent Benchmarks Measure Capability?
related.hook: An agent score only means something if the task still requires the skill it claims to test. Auditing 2,385 traces, two-thirds showed the agent taking a shortcut instead.

related.title: Chain of Thought Is a Scaling Trap? The Case for Latent Reasoning
related.hook: A visible chain of thought reads like the model's thinking — but it can be an unfaithful, expensive trace. The next wave reasons in hidden state instead of tokens.

flashcards.prompt: What assumption about LLM evaluation does this paper break?
flashcards.back_html: That model rankings are stable across inference conditions. Varying the maximum token generation budget reversed rankings on all three reasoning benchmarks tested.

flashcards.prompt: What is a 'non-monotone' item in this study?

choices.text: An item where accuracy falls as the model is allowed to generate more tokens
An item whose answer is truncated before the model finishes
An item all four models get wrong regardless of budget

flashcards.explanation_html: 3–19% of items got worse with a larger budget even after controlling for truncation — and which items behave this way is model-specific.

flashcards.prompt: What practical protocol change do the authors argue for?
flashcards.back_html: Budget-conditioned evaluation: report results across generation budgets rather than at one fixed budget, since the choice of budget can decide which model looks best.
